newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: India-Bangladesh talks on Ganges water seen crucial.
newsitem.headline: India-Bangladesh talks on Ganges water seen crucial.

text.p: Bangladesh and India will discuss sharing water from the Ganges River next week in talks which officials and analysts describe as key to future relations between the two neighbors.
"An agreement on sharing the flow of the Ganges will decide if Bangladesh should view India as a true friend," said Matiur Rahman Chowdhury, editor of Banglabazar Patrika newspaper.
Bangladesh's Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak leaves on Monday for a three-day visit to India for talks with his counterpart. Razzak also may meet with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Razzak told Reuters earlier this week he was "very optimistic" that Bangladesh and India would be able sign a long-term agreement to share water by December when the six-month dry season starts.
He said the deal was "essential for not only irrigation, navigation, environment and other water needs...but it has a strong political bearing too."
The minister said he was optimistic because of "tremendous amount of goodwill" existing in both countries for an "honourable and reasonable agreement."

However, Dr. Atiur Rahman, senior research fellow with the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies, said Bangladesh's government should "refrain from making unattainable promises to its people while negotiating a water deal with India."
"Instead it should explain the constraints. India is on the up-stream...(and) has its own needs for water. It will not just go by what Bangladesh says," he told Reuters.
Razzak said Dhaka and Delhi have many problems to sort out, but water topped the list.
The Ganges dispute has been a major irritant in relations ever since India built its Farakka barrier near Bangladesh's northern border in 1974, restricting the river's flow.
Dhaka says India diverts much of the river's water during the dry season while it releases excess water in monsoon, causing extensive flooding in Bangladesh.
Indian foreign ministry officials in New Delhi said on Wednesday the amount of water to be released during the dry season was not determined.

"People, particularly in northern Bangladesh, are facing a gradual desertification of their land, the rivers are drying, underground water levels have dropped and salinity is spreading, causing disease and crop losees," Razzak said.
Expectations for a quick resolution have risen sharply since Sheikh Hasina took office as prime minister in June following a general election that returned her Awami league to power after 21 years.

Opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), led by Hasina's predecessor Begum Khaleda Zia, has warned that it will call for a people's movement if the government failed to overcome the water shortage.
"They must bring home at least 44,000 cusecs (cubic metres per second) of Ganges water...otherwise face people's wrath," BNP's seceretary-general Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan told reporters.
Under the last agreement, which expired in 1988, Bangladesh received 34,500 cusecs during the dry season. But attempts to renew the agreement have since failed.
The quantity flowing to Bangladesh has varied from year to year since the expiry of last agreement, falling to 9,000 cusecs in March-April, 1995, according to Bangladesh water ministry officials.
